Clifford Skarstedt/Metroland Make us a preferred source on Google By Joelle Kovach Reporter Township of Douro-Dummer Mayor Heather Watson is running for re-election. Watson launched her campaign on Monday evening at Town Hall in Warsaw. She spoke to The Examiner about it on Tuesday. In her interview Tuesday, Watson mentioned projects done in the township since she was first elected mayor in 2022. These include: A floor replacement project and further upgrades totalling $2.2 million for the Douro Community Centre (expected done by September). Planning for the construction of a new $11-million combined firehall and public works building just north of Warsaw (a groundbreaking is expected this fall). Resurfacing of various roads, including County Road 4 (expected done in September). Over this last term of office, Watson said, “our council inherited a big infrastructure deficit.” ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW “You know, we started to turn things around in a positive way — and we’re building all that momentum,” she said. “I want to be able to continue to do that work and turn Douro-Dummer into a place that respects our heritage, but also is ready for the growth of the future.” More about Watson and her term as mayor Watson was first elected to township council in 2018. She was elected mayor in 2022. Her first campaign in 2022 had included a planned 50 policy commitments. At her 2026 campaign launch on Monday night, she said 44 of those commitments are either complete, substantially complete, or in progress. “That’s an 88 per cent success rate,” she said in her remarks Monday. Among her completed commitments, she made good on promises to plan the firehall and public works building, for instance, to invest in chainsaws and backup power and to update the township Emergency Response Plan. “Have we done well enough? Well, I think that 88 per cent is a solid indication that we are working hard and headed in the right direction,” she said in her speech on Monday, “Nonetheless, it is right that each of you decide for yourselves.” Watson’s take on the Alto line Alto, the federal government’s planned high-speed rail project to carry passengers from Toronto to Quebec City — with a stop in Peterborough — has left many residents of Douro-Dummer concerned about loss of farmland, the possible destruction of ecologically sensitive lands and more. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW At her campaign launch on Monday, Watson said in her remarks that “we must make clear to Transport Canada that the rail project known as Alto is not welcome in our community — and I will not support it until all of our concerns about it are fully satisfied.” In her subsequent interview, Watson told The Examiner residents remain concerned a new rail line running through part of the township might affect delivery of municipal services, for example, or emergency services. “Until there are answers” from the federal government on those details, she said on Tuesday, “I don’t support it (Alto).” “It is a ‘no’ until our concerns are satisfied,” she said. Who else is running for mayor in Douro-Dummer? J. Murray Jones, the longtime county politician who retired from public office four years ago, is running again for mayor of the Township of Douro-Dummer. Jones was first elected to Douro-Dummer township council in 1998, then mayor in 2003. He was Peterborough County Warden from 2010 to 2016 and again from 2019 to 2022. He did not seek re-election in 2022. Peter Leahy, owner of Merrylynd Organics (a farm in the Township of Douro-Dummer), is also running. Leahy told The Examiner in July that his family arrived in Peterborough just over 200 years ago, as part of a mass Irish immigration to the area. He said he was inspired to run so he can help make a better life for generations to come — just as his ancestors did. Who is running for council, in Douro-Dummer? Deputy Mayor Harold Nelson (incumbent) April Hope Councillor at large Tom Watt (incumbent) Marilyn Turton Douro Ward councillor Ray Johnston (incumbent) Rob Lyall Dummer Ward councillor Jane Cooper Nadine Ellis-Maffei Terry Little The municipal election is on Oct. 26. https://marketbusinessnews.com/why-emplo.text: Business Insights Why employers report skills shortages while young graduates struggle to find work Written by Christian Nordqvist Published: 16:25, August 23, 2026 16:25, August 23, 2026 OECD employment remained near historic highs in early 2026, yet structural labour shortages persisted while recent graduates in Australia, Canada, the European Union and the United States faced a widening unemployment gap. The apparent contradiction reflects several different problems involving skills, experience, recruitment and geography, rather than one economy-wide shortage of educated workers. The OECD Employment Outlook 2026 put the average employment rate across its member countries at 72.1% in the first quarter of the year. Unemployment was 4.9% in May. Those headline figures were strong, but momentum had weakened. The median national unemployment rate increased from 5.4% in May 2025 to 5.7% a year later, while employment growth flattened and labour shortages continued to ease from their post-pandemic peak. Young people felt more of that deterioration. Among recent university graduates aged 23 to 29, the unemployment gap with the wider working-age population had been rising since before the pandemic in every economy examined by the OECD: Australia, Canada, the EU as a weighted average and the United States. Different statistics describe different problems It helps to separate four terms that are often grouped together as a “skills mismatch”. A skills shortage occurs when employers have difficulty recruiting people with particular abilities. A skills gap exists when current employees lack some of the capabilities a business needs. A qualification mismatch occurs when somebody’s education is above, below or in a different field from the requirements of a job. A geographic mismatch places suitable workers and vacancies in different locations. The International Labour Organization uses skills mismatch as a broad term covering several of these situations. It also warns that different forms can coexist. A person can be highly qualified and still lack a job-specific skill, while somebody with the required capability may live too far from the available work. This helps explain part of the apparent paradox. Graduate unemployment measures whether people have work. An employer survey may measure difficulty filling particular vacancies. A company survey of existing staff may measure something else again. None of those statistics describes the whole labour market. Employer surveys do not measure the same shortage ManpowerGroup’s latest global survey found that 72% of employers reported difficulty finding the people they needed, down from 74% the previous year. The 2026 survey covered 39,063 employers in 41 countries. That is evidence of widespread reported hiring difficulty, but it is not an official count of unfilled vacancies. It also cannot establish whether every problem reflects a genuine scarcity of workers. Pay, working hours, location, experience requirements and recruitment practices can all affect the number of suitable applicants an employer receives. A separate OECD employer study examined firms in Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and the Slovak Republic using data collected in 2021 and 2022. More than one-third reported gaps between the skills they needed and those held by employees. Technical skills were most frequently mentioned, followed by problem-solving and teamwork. However, the gaps were usually concentrated. Fewer than 5% of firms said most or all of their workforce lacked the necessary skills. Among businesses reporting gaps, 63% said existing employees faced heavier workloads, 50% reported higher operating costs and one-third said the problem limited technology adoption. That is a different problem from a shortage of graduates. A business may have plenty of applicants but still need to train existing staff to work with new equipment, software or production methods. Experience and credentials can narrow the talent pool The difficult step for many graduates is moving from education into work. Employers value qualifications, but they also want evidence that candidates can apply knowledge in a workplace. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 found that 81% of surveyed employers expected to use work experience when assessing candidates between 2025 and 2030. Some 48% expected to use pre-employment skills tests, while 43% expected to continue using university degrees as a requirement. These are employers’ stated plans rather than observed hiring decisions. Even so, they show why a degree may open fewer doors when it is not accompanied by work experience. An employer seeking somebody who can contribute immediately may regard a graduate programme or extensive on-the-job training as an additional cost. That calculation can become self-defeating across the wider economy. If many businesses compete for experienced workers but few are willing to create that experience, recruitment difficulties can persist even when capable new entrants are available. This has encouraged interest in skills-first hiring, which gives more weight to demonstrated abilities and less to degrees or previous job titles used as proxies. The OECD’s 2026 skills-first report says the approach can widen access, particularly for people whose skills were acquired through work, short courses or informal learning. There is an important catch. Removing a degree requirement from an advertisement does not guarantee different hiring. Research cited by the OECD found that fewer than 4% of newly degree-free US job postings translated into additional hiring of people without degrees. Recruitment practices, assessment methods and managers’ decisions must change as well. Some shortages begin with the job Discussion of skills shortages often starts with what workers need to learn. Sometimes the job offer also needs attention. A 2026 European Commission working paper found that persistent shortages can be both a constraint on productivity and a symptom of poor working conditions. Low pay and low-quality jobs were particularly relevant in occupations such as care and transport. That does not mean every employer reporting difficulty should simply raise wages. Some occupations require years of training, licences or specialist experience that cannot be produced quickly. However, describing every recruitment problem as a shortage of skilled people can obscure the effect of pay, schedules, location or narrowly written job requirements. Businesses can also develop the people they already employ. In the five-country OECD study, nine in ten firms with internal skills gaps used training and staff development. Recruitment was used by 49%, while 39% changed work practices, reassigned tasks or automated parts of production. One 2025 National Bureau of Economic Research working paper shows why matching still matters after somebody is hired. Using quasi-random job assignments among new US Air Force enlistees, the researchers found that overqualified workers performed better on job-specific measures and were promoted more often, but were also more likely to leave. The military setting cannot be assumed to describe civilian workplaces, but the findings show that placing a capable person into any available job does not necessarily create a stable match. Geography and timing keep workers and jobs apart National figures can also hide large differences between local labour markets. According to the OECD’s regional analysis , the full range between the highest- and lowest-employment regions exceeded 20 percentage points in more than half of OECD economies. The average gap between regions in the top and bottom employment quintiles was 11.4 points. Moving is not a frictionless solution. Housing costs, family responsibilities, a partner’s work and access to schools can prevent a suitable applicant from relocating. Remote work removes part of the barrier for some office jobs, but it cannot place nurses in hospitals, technicians beside machinery or construction workers on building sites. Technology creates a timing problem as well. Courses take years to design and complete, while employers can introduce new software or production systems much faster. The OECD nevertheless cautions against treating generative artificial intelligence as the main explanation for the recent graduate employment problem. The deterioration began before companies started adopting large language models heavily, and the evidence on AI’s employment effects remains mixed. Employer shortages and graduate unemployment can therefore coexist without representing the same failure. Producing more graduates will not fill every specialist vacancy, while asking unemployed graduates to collect more qualifications will not create suitable work. The harder task is improving the links between education, practical experience, employer training, recruitment and the places where jobs are being created. Christian Nordqvist Christian has a love for the English Language. He spent various years as an English Language Teacher and then became an accomplished writer. He has had 80 books published, including “English for the Pharmaceutical Industry”, “English for Shipping” and “English for Law”. Prior to creating Market Business News, Christian co-founded Medical News Today and was Editor-in-Chief for the website for several years. Photograph: Mykola Tymchenko/AFP/Getty Images Kyiv Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support Attack happened shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived in city, on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing Pjotr Sauer in Kyiv Sun 4 Oct 2026 12.12 EDT First published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz , arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine. A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined. Russian drone strikes North Bridge in Kyiv, Ukraine Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter. On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. “This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.” The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, where a Russian drone strike killed two people last week . The Ukrainian president told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”. “We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said. View image in fullscreen Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/Shutterstock Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams. If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank; while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right. View image in fullscreen A Russian jet-powered drone strikes a bridge in Kyiv on 2 October. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter. “He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.” Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said. map A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv. “The EU delegation is staying,” European Union ambassador Katarina Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine,” she added. “It only reminds us why that support matters.” In Moscow, some pro-war commentators noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator. The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations. Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books Read more Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport , a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall. Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains . Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.” Explore more on these topics Kyiv Ukraine Russia Germany Friedrich Merz Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump Kyiv Independent editor: ‘Our readers want Russia to suffer but we can’t be propagandists’ Ukraine war briefing: Russia pounds power grid with seven killed in biggest energy attack in months ‘If people are in a bunker, business stops’: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses ‘This is terrorism’: daytime Russian strike hits science academy in Kyiv ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Mohammed al-Mahdi/Reuters Yemen Future of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PM Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’ Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Fri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said. Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost. Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”. View image in fullscreen Houthis ride in a funeral procession for their fellow fighters in Sana’a, Yemen, in September. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia . “We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said. Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land. ‘We expect war to reach the city soon’: Yemenis stockpile as Houthis advance on Taiz Read more Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis. He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.” Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022 . He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.” With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities. Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.” He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.” View image in fullscreen Displaced Yemeni families from al-Kadha, west of Taiz, at al-Akdaf refugee camp toward the end of last month. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes. “We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.” He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.” The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow. Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure. “Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.” He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km). He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away. In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.” He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.
